title: Great Producers of Burgundy
description: The domaines and négociants who define the standards of excellence in Burgundy today — and what makes each one special.
lessons.0.title: Understanding the Producer Landscape
lessons.0.slides.0.title: Understanding the Producer Landscape
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: 12 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Domaine vs négociant, micro-négociant, and the new generation — understanding who makes Burgundy and why it matters.
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Domaine: The Estate Model
lessons.0.slides.1.content: A Burgundy domaine grows its own grapes and makes wine from its own vineyards. The domaine model became dominant in the 20th century as growers began estate-bottling rather than selling grapes to négociants.
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Key advantage: direct control over viticulture and vinification from vine to bottle
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Fragmented land: most domaines own vines scattered across many small parcels and appellations
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Average size: most top domaines are 8–20 ha; DRC produces ~10,000 cases per year
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Risk: small size = limited production; single poor vintage impacts entire business
lessons.0.slides.2.title: Négociant: The Merchant Model
lessons.0.slides.2.content: A négociant purchases grapes, must or finished wine from growers across Burgundy, blending and labelling under their own brand. The great négociants (Bouchard, Drouhin, Jadot) also own significant vineyard holdings.
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Purchasing power: négociants can source from dozens of villages and appellations
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Blending: can select and blend across parcels for consistent style and larger volumes
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Risk: quality depends on sourcing relationships; less direct control than domaine
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Modern trend: top négociants also own vineyards; line between domaine and négociant has blurred
lessons.0.slides.3.title: The Micro-Négociant and the New Generation
lessons.0.slides.3.content: Since the 1990s, a new category has emerged: the micro-négociant, combining small domaine holdings with carefully sourced purchased grapes — often focusing on a specific style or appellation.
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Pioneers: Dominique Laurent, Jean-Marie Fourrier, Frédéric Mugnier
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Focus: micro-scale, artisanal production with extremely high precision
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.2: New wave: English-speaking trained winemakers (Alex Gambal, Thévenet) bringing fresh perspectives
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Natural wine movement: many younger producers working biodynamically with minimal intervention
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 In Burgundy, the producer matters as much as the vineyard — two estates from the same Grand Cru can produce very different wine
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Domaines control viticulture; négociants access broader sourcing
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 The distinction between domaine and négociant has blurred — the best producers combine both
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 A new generation of producers is redefining Burgundy quality from the ground up
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.question: What is the key advantage of a domaine over a négociant?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. Domaines can produce larger volumes at lower cost
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Direct control over viticulture and vinification from vine to bottle
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. Domaines are allowed to use the Grand Cru designation
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Domaines pay lower taxes than négociants
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: A domaine's fundamental advantage is direct control over the entire chain from viticulture (vine spacing, pruning, organic/biodynamic practices) through vinification. Every decision — harvest date, sorting intensity, fermentation method, élevage duration — is made by the same person who tended the vines. This integration is the source of great Burgundy's individuality.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.question: What is a key advantage of the négociant model?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. Négociants always produce wines of higher quality than domaines
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. Access to grapes from dozens of villages and appellations, enabling larger volumes and consistent supply
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. Négociants are exempt from AOC regulations
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. Négociants can use mechanical harvesting where domaines cannot
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: The négociant's purchasing relationships across Burgundy allow them to source grapes from many villages and appellations — assembling regional blends that no single domaine could achieve. This provides volume consistency, wider range, and the ability to compensate for poor harvests in one area with sourcing from another.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.question: Why does the producer's identity matter so much in Burgundy?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. Because all Burgundy Grand Crus are produced by a single cooperative
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. Because most Grand Cru vineyards are owned by multiple producers whose quality varies significantly
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. Because Burgundy producers are allowed to blend grapes from different regions
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. Because the vineyard terroir is identical for all producers in a given Grand Cru
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Most Burgundy Grand Crus are fragmented among multiple owners — for example, Clos de Vougeot has 80+ owners. Two bottles from the same vineyard can taste completely different depending on which producer made them: their viticultural practices, yield control, fermentation approach and élevage choices all profoundly shape the final wine.
lessons.1.title: Iconic Red Wine Domaines
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Iconic Red Wine Domaines
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: 18 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: The domaines that set the standard for red Burgundy — from DRC to Rousseau, Mugnier and Dujac.
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (DRC)
lessons.1.slides.1.content: The world's most celebrated wine estate. Founded by the de Villaine and Leroy families; now managed by Aubert de Villaine and co-director Frédéric Engerer. Total production approximately 10,000 cases per year across 8 Grand Cru vineyards.
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Grand Cru holdings: Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant, Grands Échézeaux, Échézeaux
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Style: biodynamic farming; whole-cluster fermentation; minimal intervention; extraordinary complexity
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Romanée-Conti price: typically €15,000–50,000+ per bottle; sold only in mixed case allocation
lessons.1.slides.2.title: Domaine Leroy (and Maison Leroy)
lessons.1.slides.2.content: Lalou Bize-Leroy is considered one of the greatest winemakers in history. Her domaine practices extreme biodynamic farming and produces from Grand Cru and Premier Cru holdings across Chambolle, Vosne, Gevrey and beyond.
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Domaine Leroy: owns Chambertin, Musigny, Clos de la Roche, Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant and more
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Philosophy: extreme low yields (10–15 hl/ha), biodynamic, hand sorting, minimal sulphur
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Prices rival DRC: Musigny from Leroy typically €15,000–30,000 per bottle
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Maison Leroy: separate négociant label — exceptional aged wines from cellars; very different from Domaine Leroy
lessons.1.slides.3.title: Armand Rousseau and Clos Saint-Jacques
lessons.1.slides.3.content: Charles Rousseau (grandson of Armand) continues the family tradition from Gevrey-Chambertin — defining what precise, elegant Gevrey Grand Cru tastes like.
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Holdings: Chambertin, Clos de Bèze, Mazis, Ruchottes, Cazetiers, Clos Saint-Jacques
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Clos Saint-Jacques (1er Cru): widely considered to produce Grand Cru quality — often exceeds Grand Cru rivals in price
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Style: precision, elegance, restrained power — not extracted or over-oaked
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Chambertin: considered one of the reference benchmarks — elegant iron and dark fruit
lessons.1.slides.4.title: Mugnier, Ponsot and Dujac
lessons.1.slides.4.content: Three domaines that define the Côte de Nuits in very different ways.
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.0: Frédéric Mugnier (Chambolle): Musigny and Bonnes-Mares — the most fragrant, silken Chambolle in the appellation
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.1: Domaine Ponsot (Morey): Clos de la Roche Vieilles Vignes — old-vine intensity; a benchmark for Morey's Grand Crus
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.2: Domaine Dujac (Morey): founded 1968 by Jacques Seysses; whole-cluster fermentation pioneer; elegant and aromatic
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.3: Dujac holdings: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Charmes-Chambertin, Bonnes-Mares, Romanée-Saint-Vivant
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.1.slides.5.points.0: 🍷 DRC and Leroy represent the two poles of Burgundy perfection — shared Grand Crus, totally different approaches
lessons.1.slides.5.points.1: 🍷 Armand Rousseau defines the Gevrey-Chambertin standard — precision over power
lessons.1.slides.5.points.2: 🍷 Mugnier = the quintessential Chambolle; Dujac = the Morey pioneer; Ponsot = old-vine Morey power
lessons.1.slides.5.points.3: 🍷 Leroy's extreme low yields and biodynamic farming produce some of the longest-lived wines in Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.6.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.question: How are DRC's wines typically sold?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.options.1: B. In mixed case allocations through appointed négociants and importers
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.options.2: C. Through annual en primeur tasting
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.options.3: D. Only at auction in Beaune
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.explanati: DRC wines are sold only through a strictly controlled allocation system — importers and négociants receive mixed cases including both the famous wines (Romanée-Conti, La Tâche) and the more accessible ones (Échézeaux). Buyers cannot purchase just the trophy wines without also taking the full case allocation.
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.question: What makes Domaine Leroy's yields exceptional?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.options.0: A. They produce the highest yields in Burgundy to achieve economies of scale
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.options.1: B. Extreme low yields of 10–15 hl/ha (versus the 35–37 hl/ha Grand Cru AOC maximum)
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.options.2: C. AOC rules require lower yields for Domaine Leroy specifically
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.options.3: D. Their biodynamic farming prevents yield control
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.explanati: Lalou Bize-Leroy's philosophy dictates extreme yield reduction — typically 10–15 hl/ha, far below the AOC Grand Cru maximum of 35–37 hl/ha and even below 'declassified' regional wine standards. This extreme concentration, combined with biodynamic farming, produces wines of extraordinary intensity and longevity.
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.question: Why is Rousseau's Clos Saint-Jacques (a Premier Cru) often discussed alongside Grands Crus?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.0: A. It is legally classified as a Grand Cru in some vintages
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.1: B. Its exceptional terroir and Rousseau's winemaking produce a wine that rivals many Grands Crus in quality and price
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.2: C. The village of Gevrey allows it to use the Grand Cru designation
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.3: D. It was recently promoted to Grand Cru by the INAO
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.explanati: Clos Saint-Jacques remains a Premier Cru by official classification, but many wine critics argue its terroir (steep slope, perfect aspect, old vines) and Rousseau's skill combine to produce wine of Grand Cru quality. It regularly commands prices exceeding many actual Grands Crus — a testament to the combination of site and producer.
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.3.question: Which domaine is credited with pioneering whole-cluster fermentation in Morey-Saint-Denis?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.3.explanati: Domaine Dujac, founded in 1968 by Jacques Seysses, was among the pioneers of whole-cluster (un-destemmed) fermentation in Burgundy — producing aromatic, silky, complex Pinot Noir with a distinctive perfumed character. Seysses trained with Henri Jayer, and his son Jeremy Seysses continues the tradition today.
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.4.question: Which two Grands Crus are DRC monopoles (exclusively owned by DRC)?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.4.explanati: Both Romanée-Conti (1.81 ha) and La Tâche (6.06 ha) are monopoles — entirely owned by DRC. They are the only two red Grand Cru monopoles in Burgundy. DRC also owns majority shares in other Grands Crus (Richebourg, Grands Échézeaux) but those are shared with other owners.
lessons.1.slides.7.title: Summary
lessons.1.slides.7.content: The great red wine domaines of Burgundy share a common thread: an obsessive attention to the vineyard, restrained intervention in the cellar, and a deep respect for terroir. From DRC's mythic Romanée-Conti to Rousseau's precise Chambertin, each domaine is an irreplaceable lens through which its terroir is interpreted.
lessons.2.title: Iconic White Wine Domaines
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Iconic White Wine Domaines
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: The producers who have defined the standard for white Burgundy — Leflaive, Raveneau, Dauvissat and Coche-Dury.
lessons.2.slides.1.title: Domaine Leflaive (Puligny-Montrachet)
lessons.2.slides.1.content: The most celebrated name in white Burgundy — producer of some of the finest Puligny-Montrachet Village, Premier Cru and Grand Cru wines. Led by Anne-Claude Leflaive until her death in 2015, now by Brice de La Morandière.
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Grand Cru holdings: Le Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet, Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Pioneer: converted entire domaine to biodynamic farming in the 1990s
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Style: pure, mineral, complex; less 'buttery' than traditional white Burgundy
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Les Pucelles (1er Cru): widely regarded as Grand Cru quality
lessons.2.slides.2.title: Raveneau and Dauvissat (Chablis)
lessons.2.slides.2.content: The two reference domaines for Grand Cru Chablis — polar opposites in style yet both equally revered.
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Jean-Marie Raveneau / Domaine Raveneau: rich, complex, oxidative style; aged in old barrel; magnificent depth
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.1: René et Vincent Dauvissat: purer, more mineral style; more restrained — the 'Leflaive of Chablis'
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Both hold Grand Cru Chablis parcels: Les Clos, Valmur, Preuses, Vaillons
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Annual production: extremely limited — fewer than 2,000 cases each; both tightly allocated
lessons.2.slides.3.title: Coche-Dury (Meursault)
lessons.2.slides.3.content: Jean-François Coche-Dury is described by many critics as the greatest white Burgundy producer alive. His Corton-Charlemagne is the most coveted of all white Burgundies.
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Style: dense, mineral, extraordinarily long-lived; both Meursault and Corton-Charlemagne
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Corton-Charlemagne price: typically €3,000–8,000 per bottle on secondary market
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Technique: no new oak for Meursault; very extended barrel aging; limited filtration
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Son Raphaël now makes the wines — same meticulously low-intervention approach
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Other Key White Producers
lessons.2.slides.4.content: Beyond the top tier, several other producers have achieved iconic status for white Burgundy.
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.0: Domaine Roulot (Meursault): Jean-Marc Roulot produces benchmark Meursault — elegant, mineral, age-worthy
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.1: Domaine Comtes Lafon (Meursault): legendary Meursault-Perrières and Le Montrachet — conversion to biodynamic 1993
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.2: Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey: rising star; produces exceptional Chevalier-Montrachet and Saint-Aubin 1er Cru
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.3: Louis Carillon (Puligny): old-fashioned, cellar-driven style; quiet but consistently excellent
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.2.slides.5.points.0: 🍷 Leflaive is the reference domaine for Puligny-Montrachet and Grand Cru white Burgundy
lessons.2.slides.5.points.1: 🍷 Raveneau and Dauvissat define the spectrum of Chablis Grand Cru style — from oxidative richness to mineral purity
lessons.2.slides.5.points.2: 🍷 Coche-Dury's Corton-Charlemagne is the most sought-after single white Burgundy wine
lessons.2.slides.5.points.3: 🍷 Biodynamic farming has been adopted by nearly every top white Burgundy domaine
lessons.2.slides.6.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.0.question: Which Domaine Leflaive Premier Cru is widely considered to be of Grand Cru quality?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.0.explanati: Leflaive's Les Pucelles (Premier Cru, Puligny-Montrachet) is consistently cited by critics as a wine that rivals or exceeds the complexity and age-worthiness of many actual Grands Crus. Its combination of premier terroir and Leflaive's biodynamic farming elevates it into Grand Cru discussion.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.question: How do the styles of Raveneau and Dauvissat in Chablis differ?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.options.0: A. Raveneau makes unoaked wines; Dauvissat uses 100% new oak
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.options.1: B. Raveneau produces rich, complex, oxidative-style Chablis; Dauvissat produces a purer, more mineral style
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.options.2: C. Raveneau produces only village Chablis; Dauvissat owns all the Grand Cru parcels
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.options.3: D. There is no meaningful difference in style between the two
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.explanati: Raveneau uses old barrels for aging, producing a richer, more complex, oxidative Chablis — deep gold, nutty, hazelnut and mineral. Dauvissat produces a more restrained, mineral, transparent style — purer, crisper, more linear. Both are considered the reference benchmarks for Chablis Grand Cru, simply at opposite stylistic poles.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.2.question: For which wine is Coche-Dury most famous?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.2.explanati: Coche-Dury's Corton-Charlemagne is their crown jewel — routinely cited as the single greatest expression of that Grand Cru, with extraordinary density, mineral tension and longevity. Secondary market prices of €3,000–8,000 per bottle reflect its legendary status, despite being sold en primeur for a fraction of that price.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.question: What farming practice has been adopted by nearly all top white Burgundy domaines since the 1990s?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.options.0: A. Intensive use of synthetic fertilisers
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.options.2: C. Mechanical harvesting for precision timing
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.explanati: Biodynamic farming, pioneered in Burgundy by Domaine Leroy (Lalou Bize-Leroy) and then Leflaive (Anne-Claude Leflaive) in the early 1990s, has been widely adopted across top white Burgundy producers. The practice emphasises soil health, biodiversity and minimal chemical intervention — reflecting a conviction that great wine begins with living soil.
lessons.3.title: Great Négociants of Burgundy
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Great Négociants of Burgundy
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: 12 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: The historic maisons de négoce — Bouchard, Drouhin, Jadot, Faiveley — and how they have redefined quality merchant Burgundy.
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Bouchard Père et Fils (est. 1731)
lessons.3.slides.1.content: One of the oldest and largest Burgundy négociants, now owned by Champagne house Henriot. Their own vineyard holdings — including some outstanding Grands Crus — span 130 ha.
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Estate holdings: Beaune-Grèves Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus (1er Cru monopole), Corton-Charlemagne, Le Montrachet, Nuits-Saint-Georges
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus: their signature wine — one of Beaune's greatest Premier Crus
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Post-Henriot acquisition (1995): major quality improvement; modern cellars and sorting
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Style: generally approachable and well-crafted; not the 'natural' school, but reliably excellent
lessons.3.slides.2.title: Joseph Drouhin (est. 1880)
lessons.3.slides.2.content: A family-run négociant of the highest calibre — one of the few major négociants where quality is truly consistent from village level to Grand Cru.
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Family-run: now in its fourth generation — Frédéric Drouhin and siblings manage the house
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Holdings: Marquis de Laguiche Le Montrachet (the largest single parcel of Le Montrachet under one name)
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Also: Griotte-Chambertin, Chambolle-Musigny Les Amoureuses (1er Cru), Clos des Mouches (Beaune)
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Biodynamic conversion ongoing; Oregon winery (Domaine Drouhin Oregon) since 1987
lessons.3.slides.3.title: Louis Jadot and Faiveley
lessons.3.slides.3.content: Two of the Côte d'Or's most important merchant-domaines, each with significant vineyard holdings complementing their négociant activity.
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Louis Jadot: now American-owned (Kobrand); 36 ha of estate vines; Clos Saint-Jacques, Chambertin, Corton-Charlemagne
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Jadot entry-level wines: among the best value consistently reliable Burgundy produced; widely available
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Faiveley: Nuits-Saint-Georges based; significant Gevrey and Chambolle holdings; Clos de Bèze, Corton-Charlemagne
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Both Jadot and Faiveley have invested heavily in improving sorting and vinification since the 2000s
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.3.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Great négociants own significant vineyard land — they are simultaneously domaine and merchant
lessons.3.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Drouhin's Marquis de Laguiche Montrachet is the most reliably outstanding single commercial parcel of Le Montrachet
lessons.3.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Bouchard's Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus is one of Burgundy's most celebrated Premier Cru red wines
lessons.3.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 All four major négociants have improved quality significantly since the 1990s through investment and biodynamic farming
lessons.3.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.question: What is Bouchard Père et Fils's signature wine?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Beaune-Grèves Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Bouchard Père et Fils's iconic wine is their Beaune Premier Cru 'Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus' — a monopole in the Les Grèves Premier Cru vineyard in Beaune. It is one of the Côte de Beaune's most celebrated red wines, combining elegance and approachability. 'L'Enfant Jésus' was the name given by Carmelite nuns who previously owned the vineyard.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.question: Why is Drouhin's Marquis de Laguiche Montrachet significant?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. It is the cheapest available Le Montrachet on the market
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. It is the largest single named parcel of Le Montrachet and consistently one of the finest
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. It is the only Le Montrachet to have biodynamic certification
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. It is a recently created single-vineyard designation
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: The Marquis de Laguiche holds the largest single parcel of Le Montrachet (~2 ha) — managed and vinified by Joseph Drouhin under a management agreement. It is consistently rated among the finest expressions of Le Montrachet, and because of Drouhin's scale it appears with slightly more frequency than smaller owners' production.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.2.question: Which of these négociants is currently American-owned?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Louis Jadot is owned by Kobrand Corporation of New York (USA), which acquired it in 1985. Despite American ownership, the house retains a strong Burgundian identity under the direction of Frédéric Barnier as head winemaker. This is a notable example of a major Burgundy négociant under foreign ownership while maintaining high quality.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.question: What is a key factor that distinguishes a top-quality négociant from a lower-quality one?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.0: A. The age of the company
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.1: B. The ownership of significant estate vineyards combined with strict sourcing relationships
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. The number of appellations they produce
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. The size of their export market
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Top négociants (Drouhin, Bouchard, Jadot, Faiveley) combine their own estate vineyard holdings (giving direct control) with carefully managed sourcing relationships with top growers. This dual structure allows quality control at both vineyard and merchant level. Lower-quality négoce buys from whoever sells most cheaply without regard for vineyard management.
lessons.3.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.3.slides.6.content: The great négociants of Burgundy are far more than mere merchants — at their finest they combine centuries of expertise, significant vineyard ownership and meticulous sourcing to produce wines that rival the finest domaines. They also play a critical role in making great Burgundy accessible across the full price spectrum.
